3883.text: In John.1.38 Jesus (party) initiates the question 'What are you seeking?' addressed to the disciples following him, making them the target party whose zēteō-activity is being probed; the operation is verbal inquiry directed at the followers' own seeking.

3912.text: In John.1.38 'What are you seeking?' is a direct, literal use of zēteō asking about the disciples' immediate purpose -- within the base gloss, no shift.

3929.text: In John.1.38 M63 (hermēneuō, 'means/interpret') co-occurs with M83 (zēteō, 'seeking') but the two operate in separate clauses -- M83 governs Jesus' question to the followers, M63 explains the term 'Rabbi'; from M83's vantage the seeking-inquiry is unrelated to the interpretive gloss on the title.

3975.text: In John.1.38 hermēneuō is used in its standard translation-gloss sense ('which means Teacher'), matching the base gloss with no notable divergence.

4201.text: In 1Sam.16.16 ('seek out a man') and 1Sam.28.7 ('Seek out...a woman') and 2Sam.17.20 ('sought and could not find'), the surface sense of procurement/search sits squarely within the base gloss with no notable shift.

4203.text: In 1Sam.16.16, the seeking operation is initiated by the servants (at the lord's command) and directed toward finding 'a man skillful in playing the lyre' -- the party sought is the skilled musician, a benign procurement operation.

4209.text: In 1Sam.16.16, M36 (servants), M15 (skillful), M24/M58 (harmful), M47 (spirit), M05/M18 (well) all co-occur; baqash's own vantage is that the seeking-out act is the mechanism by which the household responds to Saul's affliction -- the procurement operation links the human agents to the remedy, distinct from the affliction/skill terms themselves.

4256.text: In 1Sam.16.16, 'harmful spirit from God' diverges from ruach's more common empowering/animating sense (e.g. Spirit of God imparting gifts) -- here the divergence is toward an afflicting, tormenting agency; the impact is to frame Saul's distress as divinely permitted affliction requiring music as remedy.

4270.text: In 1Sam.16.16 'harmful' sits within the base gloss's 'hurtful/evil' sense (1h), a standard, unremarkable application; no notable divergence.

15084.text: Wisdom and God hate it. "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate" (Pro 8:13). Pride stands in a list with the way of evil and perverted speech.

15151.text: The Greek picture is swelling, physioō, "to inflate". In Paul it is set again and again against love: Knowledge. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Co 8:1–3). Swelling knowledge is answered not by more knowledge but by being known by God; Love is not. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4). Before this: "if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge ... but have not love, I am nothing" (13:2); Party; "that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:6–7); Here Paul states what the Hebrew verses showed in story: pride holds what was received "as if you did not receive it"; Talk without power. "Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you ... I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1Co 4:18–20). The arrogance rests on Paul being absent; Where grief belongs. "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1Co 5:2). Pride stands where mourning should be; Without reason. "puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Col 2:18–19, carried from M09); The new convert. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6). The verse joins conceit to the devil's condemnation. It does not say what the devil's condemnation was. I read: it is held for 13.3 (other spirits). It is not built on here; Controversy. "he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension" (1Ti 6:4). Conceit is joined to understanding nothing, and to quarrels; With pleasure. "swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2Ti 3:4–5); Among the others; "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Co 12:20); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26), after "let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (5:25); Conceit is named among the things that set people against each other.

Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23); Presumption acts on its own word:; the prophet "who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him" (Deu 18:20); "you would not listen; but you rebelled ... and presumptuously went up" (Deu 1:43); not obeying the decision given (Deu 17:12); The messengers mocked "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16); God works to keep pride from a person; "he opens the ears of men ... that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17); "to keep me from becoming conceited ... a thorn was given me" (2Co 12:7); The opposite named for pride is hearing, or fear; "So do not become proud, but fear" (Rom 11:20); "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance ... I hate" (Pro 8:13).

15403.text: Eze 17:14: "that the kingdom might be humble and not lift itself up, and keep his covenant that it might stand." The humble state is set by a covenant under oath. The king "rebelled … by sending his ambassadors to Egypt", and "whose oath he despised" (17:15–16). The verse names the kingdom's humbleness as the condition of its standing. The rebellion is the lifting up.

It is pursued in flight from "the love of money" (6:10); Put on: Col 3:12 (group III).

15703.text: H5753A/B (avah) makes the metaphor's two halves visible in one root split into two codes: the physical sense (bent, bowed down in pain and anguish, Isa 21:3, Ps 38:6) and the moral sense (the confession formula we have sinned and acted perversely, 1 Kgs 8:47, 2 Chr 6:37, Dan 9:5) are literally the same Hebrew word, split only for cataloguing.

15704.text: The justice and judiciary sub-theme recurs strongly: H5557 (salaph) and H5791 (avat) are both explicitly about bribery and perverting legal judgment (a bribe subverts the cause of the righteous, Exod 23:8, Deut 16:19; does God pervert justice, Job 8:3, 34:12), and H6127 and H6140 apply the same crooked language to justice itself (justice goes forth perverted, Hab 1:4; make crooked all that is straight, Mic 3:9). This is the third family, after D and G, to converge independently on judicial and legal-fairness vocabulary: corruption of justice specifically, not wrongdoing in general.

15742.text: H6601B (pathah) also appears in the heavenly-court scene where a spirit volunteers to entice Ahab to his death with God's own authorization (1 Kgs 22:20-22, repeated 2 Chr 18:19-21).

16024.text: One verb, two spirits: "a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved [*prophesied*] within his house" (1Sa 18:10) [O]; Revisit 2026-09-28 (context 1Sa 18:1–12, Batch F §1.1): this follows the day after Saul's anger at the women's song (18:8–9). In the same chapter Jonathan's soul is knit to David's. Compare the opposite order in 1Sa 11:6, where the Spirit comes first and anger follows (Batch A v3 §2.4).; "a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets" (1Ki 22:22–23) [O]

16093.text: Revisit (Batch H §2.2, §1.4) — the refusal is qualified. The law and the narratives do price a life: "The ransom of a man's life is his wealth" (Pro 13:8); "a ransom for his life … The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less" (Exo 30:12–16) — the same price for every life; "your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (1Ki 20:39) → the verdict drops the silver: "your life shall be for his life" (20:42); Satan: "All that a man has he will give for his life" (Job 2:4); [Claude reading] A life can be ransomed within the covenant, but a soul cannot be bought back from God. 16726.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Moral condition is predicated above all of the heart. The heart is: upright, whole, pure, clean or blameless (§1); evil, crooked, perverse, twisted, false or double (§2, §4, §5); proud / high or humbled / tender (§9, §10); It is also where sin is stored, engraved or hidden (§3.3). God tests and weighs it (Psa 7:9; Pro 21:2; Luk 16:15; Act 15:8). The heart is the organ that is morally evaluated.; The soul (*nephesh*) is the accountable person and the life at stake.; It sins, realises guilt, bears iniquity and is cut off (§3.1). It is the unfaithful party (§5).; It is the life that righteousness delivers (§1.7) and that sin injures (§3.2).; It is the innocent blood that is shed (§1.7). It is afflicted on holy days (§7.5).; At the limit it is the corpse that defiles (§8.2).; The soul is less often *evaluated* (righteous soul: 2Pe 2:8; puffed-up soul: Hab 2:4) than *answerable*.; The human spirit is evaluated chiefly on the pride–humility axis (§9.2, §10.2): haughty, proud, hardened, lowly, poor, contrite. Otherwise it is: without deceit (Psa 32:2); right / clean (Psa 51:10); faithful in marriage (Mal 2:15–16); trustworthy (Pro 11:13); holy or defiled with the body (1Co 7:34; 2Co 7:1); sanctified with soul and body (1Th 5:23); perfected in the righteous dead (Heb 12:23); weighed (Pro 16:2); broken by a perverse tongue (Pro 15:4); [observation, not a count]; Other spirits carry the negative moral adjectives. They are evil / harmful (§2.1, 15 verses), unclean (§8.1, 23 verses) and lying / deceitful (§4.1, 6 verses). They are the moral clusters' names turned into kinds of spirit.; In the OT some are sent by God (1Sa 16; Judg 9:23; 1Ki 22:22–23).; In the NT they indwell and are cast out.; The Holy Spirit is the positive counterpart, and the one against whom human sin is directed: blasphemed, lied to, grieved, resisted, outraged (§2.4, §4.2, §7.1).; Inner vs outer purity.; Ritual clean / unclean / holy vocabulary attaches to flesh, body and *nephesh*-as-person or corpse.; Moral purity attaches to heart, spirit, soul and conscience.; Several texts deliberately contrast the two: Psa 24:4; 2Ch 30:19; Mar 7:19–21; Heb 9:13–14; 10:22; Jam 4:8.

18904.text: What it is. Knowing that cannot close: a mind held open before something it cannot interpret. The bearers are all human: Herod (Mar 6:20; Luk 9:7), the disciples (Joh 13:22), the women at the tomb (Luk 24:4), the Pentecost crowd (Act 2:12), the temple captain and chief priests (Act 5:24), Peter (Act 10:17), Paul (2Cor 4:8; Gal 4:20), Festus (Act 25:20), and Belshazzar's lords (Dan 5:9).

18905.text: What carries it instead of a seat: the question spoken aloud: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9, context); the gaze: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22); a reflexive pronoun: Act 10:17 "inwardly perplexed" is *en heautō*, "in himself". The inner location is there, but through a pronoun, not a seat word.; the body of the other party: in Dan 5:6 the king's "color changed … his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together". The body tells the alarm while his lords are perplexed.

18906.text: Before and after. Perplexity is a waiting state that something from outside ends: Luk 24:4, "While they were perplexed … behold, two men stood by them"; Act 10:17–19: the men arrive at the gate, and the Spirit speaks; Act 2:12–14: "But Peter, standing … lifted up his voice"; Dan 5:10–12: the queen names Daniel; The operation rarely resolves from within. An interpreter arrives.

18908.text: How the sense shifts. In Mar 6:20, Herod "feared John, knowing … greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly". Four inner operations sit on one bearer with no seat word, each named by a word from a different cluster (fear M01, knowing M15, gladness M04). The operations name themselves. In Gal 4:20 the perplexity is love's: it comes straight after "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth" (4:19).

19236.text: Who bears it: Herod (Mar 6:20; Luk 9:7); the disciples (Joh 13:22); the women at the tomb (Luk 24:4); the Pentecost crowd (Act 2:12); the temple captain and chief priests (Act 5:24); Peter (Act 10:17); Festus (Act 25:20); Paul (2Cor 4:8; Gal 4:20); Belshazzar's lords (Dan 5:9).

19237.text: Where it comes from. Something heard or seen that exceeds the categories at hand: "it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead" (Luk 9:7); "we hear them telling in our own tongues" (Act 2:11–12); "what the vision … might mean" (Act 10:17); an empty tomb (Luk 24:3–4); Jesus's "one of you will betray me" (Joh 13:21–22); writing on a wall no one could read (Dan 5:8–9)

19238.text: What it does. It asks aloud: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9). It looks at others: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22). It turns inward: "Peter was inwardly [*en heautō*, in himself] perplexed" (Act 10:17). Festus hands the question on: "Being at a loss how to investigate … I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem" (Act 25:20).

19239.text: How it co-exists.; Herod: "Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man … When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly" (Mar 6:20). Fear, knowledge, perplexity and gladness are all present in one man towards one prophet, and the perplexity keeps him listening.; Amazement: "all were amazed and perplexed" (Act 2:12).; The body of another man: Belshazzar's "color changed … his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6) while his lords were perplexed (5:9).; Anguish of love: "I am perplexed about you" (Gal 4:20), after "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth" (4:19).; A limit held: "perplexed, but not driven to despair" (2Cor 4:8). The perplexity is bounded, and the neighbouring verses set it inside "God … has shone in our hearts" (4:6) and "this treasure in jars of clay" (4:7).

19240.text: What it leads to. Mostly, something from outside ends it: "While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them" (Luk 24:4); "the men … stood at the gate" and "the Spirit said to him" (Act 10:17, 19); "Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice" (Act 2:14); the queen names Daniel (Dan 5:10–12); Herod "sought to see him" (Luk 9:9); Perplexity ends when an interpreter or a meeting arrives.

19241.text: Seat.; In the verse: none of the 11 names a seat. The operation word names itself (v1 §1.1, §3 item 1). Act 10:17 locates it with a reflexive pronoun, *en heautō*, "in himself", which is not an M47 word (v1 §3 item 6).; In the passage, the other party's (genuine): Joh 13:22 ← 13:21 "Jesus was troubled in his spirit". The seat is Jesus's, and the perplexity is the disciples' (v1 §1.1).; In the passage, the bearer's own (genuine): 2Cor 4:8 ← 4:6 "God … has shone in our hearts" (v1 §1.1). The bounded perplexity sits inside hearts already lit.; In the passage, the interpreter's — new in v3: Dan 5:9 → 5:12 "an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found in this Daniel". The lords are perplexed and have no seat. The seat that arrives belongs to the interpreter, and it is named as the very capacity the perplexed lack. This gives v2's finding a seat. Perplexity ends when an interpreter arrives, and in Daniel's case the text locates the interpreter's gift in his spirit.; Divine Spirit: Act 10:17 → 10:19 "the Spirit said to him". That is the other party, and divine. It ends the perplexity from outside.

19680.text: 2 Corinthians 8:17 — "being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord": The chapter is about giving to the poor saints. It opens with the Macedonians: *"in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity"* (v2). They gave *"according to their means … and beyond their means, of their own accord"* (v3). That is the same word as in v17 (G0830, *authairetos*, "self-chosen"). The order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (v5). Their own accord and the will of God stand side by side in one sentence.; Paul will not command the Corinthians: *"I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine"* (v8). He presses them on the gap between wanting and doing: *"finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it"* (v11); *"if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has"* (v12). The readiness (G4288) and the desiring (G2309) have to be matched by completing.; Titus is described the same way: *"thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (v16–17). The verse holds three things together: God put the care into his heart (G1325, G2588); he accepted the appeal; he goes of his own accord, out of his own earnestness (G4705); The text does not set them against each other or explain how they fit. I read it as saying that what God put into the heart became Titus's own, so that he goes because he wants to.; The outcome is stated only as his going. Another brother is sent who is *"more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you"* (v22). The aim is that the giving be honourable *"not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man"* (v21).

19688.text: Own accord alongside God's working. Titus goes *"of his own accord"* after God *"put into the heart"* the care (2Cor 8:16–17). The Macedonians give *"of their own accord"*, having given themselves to the Lord *"by the will of God"* (8:3, 5). Both are named and neither cancels the other. This sits with batch 2 (the way to choose is taught) and the test (Psa 119:32, the heart enlarged by God).

19748.text: G0830, of one's own accord: "they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord" (2Cor 8:3); "being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord" (2Cor 8:17)

19838.text: G0830, "of one's own accord". One word, literally "self-chosen" (2Cor 8:3, 17).

19856.text: Own accord, and God at work: Two things are named side by side and not set against each other: *"thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you"*; *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2Cor 8:16–17); The Macedonians gave *"of their own accord"*, and the order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (8:3, 5). The church's choice is joined to the Spirit's in the same verb: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (Act 15:28). The psalmist chooses, and asks God to give the room to carry it out: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (Psa 119:32). I read these verses as saying that what God puts into the heart becomes the person's own. The verses name both and do not explain how they fit.

19956.text: Seeking, and not obtaining. *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Rom 11:7). The rest were seeking. They were given *"eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear"* (11:8). Paul at once refuses the conclusion that this is the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11). The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not works (11:5–6). The passage says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

21304.text: Call is God's own act of summoning, choosing or appointing a person or people; it bears on their inner response (faith, obedience, hope), which other words of the verse name, and is the outward act upon them.

21306.text: Call here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21384.text: New gives freshness to a song of praise: the praise of the person is voiced afresh to the Lord.

21461.text: Holy is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).

21469.text: Righteous is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).

21489.text: Ungodly is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.

21505.text: Wicked is here the wickedness, ungodliness or sinfulness of a person as a state or practice of the heart, set against godliness and what is right (ungodliness, a heart busy with iniquity, a wicked deed, sinful passions).

21507.text: Wickedly here names an attribute of God or of his rule (a righteous Lord, the scepter of uprightness, the Holy One, his holy name or Spirit, the mystery of godliness); no operation of a person's inner being is voiced by it.
